## 23. Kotlin libraries design

Two Android library modules in the Gradle build at `android/sdk/` (PD16, PD19), `minSdk 29` (PD11) on arm64-v8a with FP16, `compileSdk 37` (the emulator image's API level, `evidence/03-device-feasibility.md` Method).

| Module | Change | What |
|---|---|---|
| `:core` (`io.github.christopherlinnett.craftbridge:core`) | NEW | generated core bindings, the Kotlin core API, `NativeSurfaces` (JNI, §20); depends on JNA (`net.java.dev.jna:jna`, `@aar`) |
| `:effects` (`io.github.christopherlinnett.craftbridge:effects`) | NEW | generated EffectCraft bindings and facade, the hand-written fixed-shape calls, and in `jniLibs/{arm64-v8a,x86_64}/` the library the layer table gives the SDK (§15), `libcraftbridge_effects_ffi.so` while it has one app |
| `:effects` `androidTest` | NEW | instrumented conformance tests on the emulator (QA-2) |

**Device floor.** The arm64 library is built for half-precision arithmetic in every crate (`-C target-feature=+fp16`, `tools/env.sh`), so it needs a processor that has it: ARMv8.2-A, Cortex-A55 and A75 and newer. `EffectsEngine.start` on an arm64 phone without it throws the `Unsupported` exception the core answers, whose message names the missing feature (`HWCAP_FPHP` or `HWCAP_ASIMDHP`), before any engine code runs; an app catches it and tells its user that the app's video engine needs a newer processor than the phone has. The x86_64 emulator takes no half-precision path and starts.

**Kotlin API.** Mirrors §22: `EffectsEngine.start(context, folders, gpu)`, which starts through the core's `Engine.start(folders, begin)`: that reads `MediaCodecList(REGULAR_CODECS)` first and hands each codec's name, types, `isEncoder` and `isHardwareAccelerated()` to `set_device_codecs` (§18), so the engine registers the hardware decoders the device lists; `suspend` functions, progress as a lambda, cancellation through the coroutine's `Job`. Each of §5's calls lives in one place: `exec`, `run`, `props`, `get`, `set`, `frame`, `export`, `replay`, `timings` and `mcp` are members of `EffectsEngine`, each a thin call into the one method of §14's table that answers it, over `:core`'s request with progress where the method reports one, and the engine is ended by its `shutDown`; `templates.open` and `templates.render` are hand-written extensions of the generated `TemplatesCommands` type, because `templates` is a generated namespace and these answer the plugin's `template.open` and `template.render` methods beside the namespace's commands. `templates.open` answers the same `TemplateInstance` as §22, whose `set(name, value)` and `set(name, media)` run the commands `template.open`'s own values run — `essential.set` on the instance, in its own composition, after `file.import` for a media file, which is a `File` so that no text value is ever read as a path — since §14's table has no method that sets a control of an instance already open. A public call written by hand never takes the name of a public call the facade generates on the same type, neither a namespace's word on `EffectsEngine` nor a command's name on a namespace's type: Kotlin refuses only a member property beside an extension property of its name, and detekt's `GeneratedNameTaken` refuses every form (AGENTS §9). The generated namespaces answer every command an app can call (§21). `script` has no phone method (PD13). `Folders.appDefault(context)` uses `filesDir`, `cacheDir` and `noBackupFilesDir`, and names its `staged` folder beside `config` and `models` — never under the `cacheDir`, which the system may empty while the app is not running and a saved project must still find the copies it names; an app's assets are copied to `filesDir` before use, because the engine reads files, not asset streams. The preview and the pictures have a typed call each on `EffectsEngine`, over the core's `Engine`, which an app reaches as `EffectsEngine.core`: `preview(surface, comp = …, time = …)` attaches the app's `Surface` when the engine is not previewing into this one yet — the first call, a new surface, a `Surface` that names another window since (a `SurfaceView` hands out one object for every surface it makes), or after `endPreview()` or a GPU that took the surface with it — and draws the comp at the time into it, so an app that draws many frames into one surface names that surface on every call and it is attached once; `preview(comp = …, time = …)` draws into the surface already attached. The preview's `time` is a `kotlin.time.Duration`, which the typed call turns into the seconds the engine speaks in one place, as Swift turns its `Duration` (§22), and `endPreview()` gives the surface up, so the next `preview` of any surface attaches afresh. `frameBitmap(…)` answers a `Bitmap` (`ARGB_8888`, premultiplied) and `frameHardwareBuffer(…)` a `HardwareBuffer` from Android 12 (§17), each taking `frame`'s own arguments. The four build the one request, through `frameRequest`, in the fields the engine's `frame` reads, the preview's `previewRequest` the one place a named `Duration` becomes the engine's seconds, and hand it to the core's `present`, `frameBitmap`, `frameHardwareBuffer` and `frame`, so no call spells the request a second time and an app writes no JSON. The core's `Engine` holds the calls under them: `attachPreview(surface: Surface)`, `present(params)`, `detachPreview()` and `hasPreviewSurface()`, which answers from the core, on the engine thread and so behind a lost device settled, whether a preview surface is held — the one report both bindings ask — beside `holdsPreview(surface)`, its report read together with the window the app attached last, whose address it compares with that of the window the surface names now (`window_address`, §20), which is what a typed `preview` asks before attaching, the attach, the detach and that reading each made under one lock, so two attaches at once leave the window remembered the one the engine took last; with `suspendGpu()` and `resumeGpu()`, which drops the surface and so needs it attached again, and `frameBitmap(params)` and `frameHardwareBuffer(params)`, whose `params` is the request's JSON text. The same `Engine` keeps a `recovery()` pass-through beside those calls, answering what a start cleaned up after an export the system killed (§16, D-17), the boundary's own report unchanged. `attachPreview` takes the surface's window through `NativeSurfaces` (JNI, §20), which loads the library with `System.loadLibrary` because the JVM looks an `external fun` up in the libraries it loaded itself, and JNA's own `dlopen` is no such load; it loads it under the name the core's bindings load it by, from their own lookup, so the library is named once, from the layer table.

**Build.** `tools/build-android.sh` takes the library the layer table gives the SDK (§15; `craftbridge-effects-ffi` while it has one app) from `cargo xtask sdk-library`, its package and its library's name, and runs `cargo ndk -t arm64-v8a -t x86_64 -o android/sdk/effects/src/main/jniLibs build --release -p <package>` at the module's minSdk with NDK r28, which aligns to 16 KB pages by default (`evidence/05-mobile-platforms.md` Finding 11), the aarch64 library with the `fp16` target feature (LLVM's `fullfp16`) gemm-f16 needs (never the host's `native`), the NDK and the feature set once in `tools/env.sh` for the script, the gate's mobile stage and a device run alike. It then checks the alignment of each built library (`cargo xtask elf-alignment`, V6) and runs `cargo xtask generate`, whose registered generators write the Kotlin bindings into each module's `src/generated/kotlin/` (§20). JNA is an `@aar` dependency of `:core`, which the convention plugin hands out in place of the jar the POM names, and `:core`'s consumer R8 rules, which `:effects` takes with it, keep what JNA reaches by reflection and from native code in the bindings. The generated bindings declare no visibility on their helpers, which explicit API mode refuses, so each file suppresses those two diagnostics for itself, and the convention plugin quiets the compiler's warning about suppressing an error, which no setting narrower than the whole compilation can; detekt makes that refusal instead on every file but the bindings', so the facade beside them and the written code keep the mode whole. The library lookup UniFFI writes private to each file (`findLibraryName`) is made visible to its module, for `NativeSurfaces`.

**Build setup.** `gradle/libs.versions.toml` holds every version and `build-logic` the setup every module shares: AGP 9 with its built-in Kotlin, explicit API mode, Kotlin and Android Lint warnings as errors, Spotless with ktlint, and detekt with the build's own rules (`build-logic/detekt-rules`), registered over every variant and test component (D-28). A module's build file holds only its convention plugin, its namespace and its dependencies, and `cargo xtask rules` refuses any other statement (AGENTS §10, decision #121); `settings.gradle.kts` fails the build for a module that does not apply the convention plugin, which would otherwise build without those rules; the plugin reads its rules back once a module's build file has run, so that file cannot set them back; the settings refuse a gate check whose working tasks a build file has unhooked, the Android stage a task one has disabled, and `cargo xtask rules` a `lint.xml`, which would switch Lint checks off for its folder (D-25). A module's tasks take turns at its build folder, through a build service one task holds at a time: Gradle deletes the folders a skipped task's old outputs leave empty, AGP's sibling tasks keep their outputs under folders they share, and the configuration cache runs a project's tasks in parallel, so without turns a module that loses its last sources fails the build on some runs and not others.

**Publishing.** `maven-publish`, configured once in `build-logic`, publishes release builds only to `https://maven.pkg.github.com/ChristopherLinnett/craftbridge` with the ChristopherLinnett token (PD3), at the version `rust/Cargo.toml` gives, which the release script hands in as the `craftbridge.version` property; without it every publish task refuses to run, since a publication with no version of its own would go out as Gradle's `unspecified` (§26, G2, D-27). The published metadata says what a consumer's resolver cannot read off the coordinates alone: `:core`'s dependency on JNA names its AAR — the POM's `type` and Gradle's own artifact selector in the module metadata, because JNA's own POM names only the jar — and the POM of an artifact that packages a native library, `:effects`, states the ABIs it is built for (`arm64-v8a`, `x86_64`), read from the `jniLibs` folders AGP packages rather than written down again, in its properties and description, which is where AGP lets them be said. A local proof folder, named by a property, writes the publication beside GitHub so a release run checks its own metadata first.

**Tests.** Each module's unit tests on the host (`testDebugUnitTest`, on TestNG), and `./gradlew :effects:connectedAndroidTest` on the emulator, in the gate; on the two acceptance Android phones (QA-3). Two device checks run inside an app, which no `adb shell` run can: the export's thread pool equals the rule of AD7 at 1080p, 4K, 5K and 8K for the `MemAvailable` the app reads (a size one frame of it at the rule's copies does not fit the device's free memory at all left out and said, and, on a device whose memory runs every named size on all its cores, a square size of its own whose rule gives half of them, since only a pool below the cores shows an export sized by the memory), and an engine started through the SDK meets the FP16 floor with the capability bits the app reads from `/proc/self/auxv`.
